title: Woodward Topples Caruana; Lee On 4.5/5 After Bloodiest Day Yet
summary: Eight out of 12 games were decisive on Wednesday, making it the bloodiest round across both tournaments in this year's 2026 U.S. Chess Championships. GM Andy Woodward took down defending champion GM Fabiano Caruana to join GM Wesley So in the lead on 3.5/5. So drew GM Grigoriy Oparin. The other three winners were GM Jeffery Xiong (against GM Levon Aronian), GM Ray Robson (against GM Hans Niemann), and GM Abhimanyu Mishra (against GM Sam Sevian). Seventeen-year-old IM Alice Lee leads the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship by a full point after beating IM Tatev Abrahamyan with the black pieces to land on the nearly perfect 4.5/5 score. Her closest trailers are WIM Rachael Li (who beat WGM Jennifer Yu), FM Megan Paragua (who beat IM Nazi Paikidze), and WGM Thalia Cervantes (after a draw with GM Irina Krush). IM Rose Atwell won a brilliancy against defending champion IM Carissa Yip but is on 2/5. Round six is on Thursday, October 15, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 5: Open Standings After Round 5: Women Round 5 Results: Open There were just two draws in each tournament. In the open section, the draws were in Oparin vs. So and GM Awonder Liang vs. GM Sam Shankland. So held a Berlin Defense to stay in pole position, and Shankland's Dragon Sicilian still petered out to an equal endgame. Liang is a half-point behind the leaders, while Shankland is a full point back. The Game of the Day was, without a doubt, Woodward's win against Caruana with a slow, positional squeeze in the QGD Ragozin Variation. The teenager confirmed with GM Maurice Ashley that it was his career-best win, saying, "I've beaten some low 2700s, but this was the first time beating Fabi." He made fantastic use of the bishop pair advantage, and even though the conversion wasn't engine-perfect, it was enough to beat the third-highest-rated player of all time. title: Roman Shogdzhiev, 11, Closes In On Mishra's Youngest GM Record
summary: IM Roman Shogdzhiev took a major step toward becoming the youngest grandmaster in chess history on Monday, scoring his second GM norm in the Serbian Super League. The 11-year-old is now one norm and 29 rating points away from breaking GM Abhimanyu Mishra's 2021 record. The prodigy had an incredible run in the team tournament, playing on board one for Partizan Belgrade. He defeated strong GMs Ivan Cheparinov (2631), Bharath Subramaniyam (2603), and Jingyao Tin (2602). Shogdzhiev finished his tournament by drawing Hungarian GM Ferenc Berkes in round nine on Monday to reach 6/9. Shogdzhiev sat out the final two rounds, finishing with a performance rating of 2662, comfortably above the 2600 required for a GM norm. He also gained 26.1 rating points, taking his live rating to 2471.1. Shogdzhiev displayed impressive fighting spirit throughout the tournament, grinding out wins in the endgame. His most impressive victory, however, was against four-time Bulgarian champion Cheparinov, who currently works with super GM Alireza Firouzja. In that game, he was in control from start to finish.

title: World Championships U7–U17 2026: Young talents make their mark in Spain
summary: Surprises and perfect scores shape the opening rounds of the 2026 World Championships U7–U17 With an outstanding turnout of 721 players representing 82 countries, the 2026 FIDE World Championships U7–U17 got underway on October 13 in the coastal town of Roquetas de Mar, in the province of Almería, southern Spain. Running until October 21, the event is jointly organized by the International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Spanish Chess Federation and is being held at the Evenia Zoraida Beach Resort. The competition features 12 age categories: Under 7, Under 9, Under 11, Under 13, Under 15 and Under 17, with separate Open and Girls sections in each age group. Many national delegations are represented across all six age groups, highlighting the breadth of participation at this year’s championships. Kazakhstan, for example, has players competing in every age category, underlining the importance of the event as a platform for developing young chess talent. As is customary in tournaments of this kind, the championships follow an 11-round Swiss system. The main innovation this year is the time control: each player receives 45 minutes for the entire game, with a 30-second increment per move from move one. Following several successful pilot events, this *fast classical* format is being introduced for the first time in an official youth championship, with all games counting towards FIDE ratings. The new time control aims to offer a more dynamic playing experience while retaining the strategic depth of classical chess. Representing FIDE, Ozgur Solakoglu (Technical Delegate), officially opened the championships, welcoming all participants and wishing them every success and an enjoyable competition. Javier Ochoa de Echagüen, president of the Spanish Chess Federation, acknowledged that many players had travelled long distances to take part in the event. He expressed his hope that they would enjoy their stay at the resort and perform to the best of their abilities over the coming days. Finally, International Arbiter Panagiotis Nikolopoulos reviewed some of the main rules and regulations and reminded players of the tournament schedule. With the formalities completed, he started the clocks for the first of the two rounds scheduled for the opening day. As is customary in Swiss-system tournaments, where the top seeds are generally paired against lower-rated opponents in the early rounds, most of the favourites made a strong start. However, there were a few surprises, particularly in the youngest age groups. The Under 7 Open section is especially unpredictable, with more than half of the participants yet to receive a FIDE rating. With so many players still establishing their competitive strength, the opening rounds offer plenty of scope for unexpected results and emerging talents to make their mark. Under 7 (53 players in the open section and 28 players in the girls’ section) The youngest participants play in a dedicated room adapted to their needs, with a spacious waiting area nearby where parents can easily collect their children as soon as their games finish. After two rounds, the top two seeds in the Under 7 Open section, Spain’s Pau Vizcaya Lopez and Egypt’s Mohab Ahmed Assem, are among a group of 10 players who have won both their games and share the lead with a perfect 2/2 score.  In the Girls’ section, five players have also won both games. Uzbekistan’s Malika Ikromova tops the standings on tiebreak. Under 9 (82 players in the open section and 40 players in the girls’ section) In the Girls’ section, second seed Varvara Volkova, competing under the FIDE flag, holds the top position on tiebreak. Five other players have also won their first two games, including Finland’s Stella Zhu, the highest-rated participant in the field. In the Open section, 14 players share the lead with a perfect score after two rounds, headed by Latvia’s Akims Jefimovs. Top seed Wiktor Stankowski of Poland has already dropped half a point and sits just behind the leaders. Under 11 (99 players in the open section and 47 players in the girls’ section) Candidate Master Amirzhan Anetov leads the Under 11 Open section after winning both of his games, with 14 other players close behind on a perfect score. Seeds two to five have all dropped points, underlining the strength of the field and suggesting that several young competitors may be underrated. In the Girls’ section, only six players have maintained a perfect score after two rounds. Israel’s Arbel Ben Ari is the surprise leader on tiebreak, despite being ranked just 43rd among the 47 participants at the start of the tournament. Under 13 (75 players in the open section and 43 players in the girls’ section) WFM Alina Donets, representing Austria, leads the Under 13 Girls’ section on tiebreak, although she shares a perfect score with seven other players. In this category, most of the top seeds have lived up to expectations, demonstrating their strength in the early rounds. The Under 13 Open section is even more tightly contested, with 15 players sharing the lead on 2/2. While the top seeds remain in contention, it is surprise performer Saravanan Keertieshvar, seeded 53rd, who currently tops the standings. Unfortunately, the second and fourth seeds, both FIDE Masters representing Syria, have yet to arrive in Spain. They are expected to join the competition tomorrow, but will have to begin their campaigns from zero points after missing the opening rounds. Under 15 (85 players in the open section and 43 players in the girls’ section) In the Under 15 Open section, 16 players have won both their games, including the six highest-ranked masters in the category. Kazakhstan’s Zhanbolat Amankos deserves special mention after producing one of the biggest upsets of the round by defeating Austria’s FM Florentin Stickler. In the Under 15 Girls’ section, local player Amaya Alfaro Aldunate scored an impressive second-round victory over Turkey’s WCM Arya Aydogan. She is among nine players who have started the tournament with two wins from two games. WFM Aiaru Altynbek currently leads the group on tiebreak. title: FIDE World Junior U20 Championship in Venezuela: Registration deadline extended
summary: FIDE and the Venezuelan Chess Federation, in cooperation with the Ministry of People’s Power for Sport, invite all FIDE Member Federations to participate in the FIDE World Junior U20 Championship to be held in Caracas 17 to 28 November 2026. Each National Federation may register up to two invited players (one per category). Additional players may be sent at the federation’s own expense. Players holding personal participation rights under FIDE Regulations are also eligible as invited players: Top three players of the 2025 World Junior Championships; Continental Junior Champions of the year preceding this edition; Top six Junior U20 players (Open) and top four (Girls) from the FIDE Rating List as of 1 January 2026; World Youth Under-18 and Under-16 Champions of the year preceding this edition By agreement with the Venezuelan organizers, the registration deadline (including visa support requests) has been extended from October 16 to October 30, 2026. All registrations must be submitted through the respective National Federation using the official registration form.  Security Measures The Organizing Committee, in close coordination with FIDE, reaffirms its commitment to the well-being of all participants and visitors during their stay in Caracas and announces the following protocols: National Security Measures: Coordination with state security forces to ensure a secure corridor, hotel security, and continuous surveillance of the playing hall. Included Medical Insurance: Comprehensive health and medical insurance for every accredited participant for the duration of the event. Emergency Response Service: Primary medical care center and a 24-hour ambulance at the venue. Controlled Transfers: Official transport exclusively for airport-hotel-airport transfers and tournament-related activities. For further information, please contact: worldjunior@fide.com Attachments: Official statement by the organizing committee of FIDE World Junior U20 Championship (PDF) Registration form (PDF)

title: Ticket sales for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship are now open
summary: The most anticipated chess event of the year, the match for the world crown, opens on 22 November in Geneva, Switzerland, with the first game scheduled for 24 November. Two 20-year-old prodigies, World Champion Gukesh D of India and Challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will battle for the World Championship title and the right to be called the leader of their generation. Seeing the players up close, feeling the tension and emotions of the match, and socialising with fellow chess fans and grandmaster guests is an unmatched experience for any chess enthusiast. Ticket sales open today! There are two types of tickets available: the VIP Day Pass, which includes an hour in the playing hall, and the Fan Zone Pass. The Fan Zone will be packed with different activities, simuls, tournaments, master classes and Q&A with grandmasters (on selected days), opportunities to play chess, photo opportunities, and a live broadcast from the playing hall on the big screen. Due to the strictly limited number of VIP Passes, holders will enjoy an exclusive view of the games from the balcony overlooking the playing hall, allowing them to experience its palpable silence. It also grants access to all the perks of the VIP Lounge, including live commentary by GMs Peter Svidler and Peter Leko. The number of tickets is limited, and they will be released in stages with dynamic pricing. So don’t wait until the last moment; get your tickets now!
